tcp.conn_bytes_limit: Despite the name, this counts PACKETS, not bytes. b4 only sends the first N packets of each TCP connection through userspace inspection (the handshake/early-payload window); the rest stay on the kernel fast-path. Default 19, hard max 100. The cap is enforced at the nftables level via 'ct original packets < N+1'. Higher values let b4 apply DPI bypass to longer-lived flows but cost CPU and add latency to every connection. Lower values shrink the inspection window and may miss late TLS-handshake patterns the bypass logic depends on.
tcp.seg2delay: Milliseconds b4 waits AFTER sending segment 1 (first part of a split) BEFORE sending segment 2 (the rest). Used by the dominant two-segment splits: extsplit, firstbyte, tls, and DNS fragmentation. Defeats DPI middleboxes that read both segments within a single read window and reassemble them into one logical record before inspecting. The min/max range form randomizes the wait to evade timing fingerprints. In disorder mode (multi-segment splits) the same value is reused as the gap between every consecutive segment pair. Cost: every wait adds to TLS-handshake latency. Setting min and max to 0 disables the wait (fastest, but some DPI engines reassemble split segments anyway and the bypass loses effect).
tcp.dport_filter: Comma-separated list of TCP destination ports and ranges this set targets. Examples: '443', '80,443,5222', '1000-2000', or combinations. Empty means the set has no port-list contribution; b4 always queues port 443 by default regardless of any set's filter, so an empty filter still gets you 443. Each enabled set's DPortFilter values are unioned into the nftables 'tcp dport {...}' queue rule, so listed ports are sent to b4 userspace and unlisted ports stay on the kernel fast-path entirely. Used both for kernel-level filtering AND userspace per-set matching.
tcp.drop_sack: Strips the TCP SACK option (kind 5) AND the SACK-Permitted option (kind 4) from outgoing packets b4 reinjects. SACK-Permitted lives in the SYN, so removing it prevents the connection from negotiating SACK at all - both endpoints fall back to plain ACKs. Used to neutralize DPI that fingerprints clients by SACK behavior or treats SACK negotiation as a 'real client' signal. Side effect: throughput suffers on lossy links because retransmits become full-window resends instead of selective. Only applied when b4 is already reinjecting the packet for other reasons (fragmentation, faking, desync, etc.); has no effect on packets that pass through unmodified.
tcp.duplicate: Targeted feature: sends multiple copies of each matching packet to specific destination IPs (configured via the duplicate IP set, not all traffic). 'count' is how many copies are sent, range 1-10, default 3. Helps against DPI that probabilistically drops packets - extra copies improve the odds at least one survives the path. Costs: bandwidth multiplier on the destination, and some servers reject what looks like duplicate-segment retransmits. Only takes effect on packets going to the configured duplicate IP set; enabling this without populating the IP set changes nothing.
tcp.ip_block_detect: Detects when a destination is being silently IP-blocked by ISP-level DPI (the connection just hangs because nothing comes back) and fails it fast on the local side. Without this, the user's browser spins for 30+ seconds before giving up; with it, the user gets an immediate connection error and can retry or take a different route. If cache_blocked_ips is set, b4 remembers blocked destinations and fails subsequent connections to them immediately rather than waiting for the same evidence to accumulate again. Also feeds the Escalate.To chain - if the set has an escalation target, the blocked host is moved to that next set's bypass strategy instead of (or in addition to) failing fast. Watches HTTPS connections only.
tcp.ip_block_detect.retransmit_threshold: Sensitivity knob for ip_block_detect. Default 3, range 1-10. Lower values make b4 declare blocks faster (better responsiveness, more false positives on lossy links where retransmits are normal). Higher values are more tolerant (fewer false positives but the user waits longer before getting a fast-fail or strategy escalation). Threshold of 1 is dangerous - a single dropped packet on the path is enough to trigger a full block. Each connection is counted independently, so unrelated traffic doesn't influence detection on a different destination.
tcp.rst_protection: Drops incoming RST packets that look like middlebox injections rather than legitimate server resets. Without this, a single injected RST closes the connection and the bypass attempt fails. b4 distinguishes injected RSTs from legitimate ones using several signals derived from the RST and the connection's prior state; if the signals point to injection, the RST is dropped and the connection survives. Subsequent legitimate RSTs from the real server still close the connection normally. Also feeds the Escalate chain: when enough RSTs are dropped within Escalate.RstWindowSec, the host is escalated to the next set's bypass strategy.
tcp.rst_protection.ttl_tolerance: Tolerance knob for one of the rst_protection signals (TTL-based). Default 3, range 1-20. Lower = stricter detection of injected RSTs (more middlebox RSTs caught, but also a higher chance of dropping legitimate RSTs after a route change). Higher = more lenient (fewer false drops of legitimate RSTs, but more middlebox RSTs slip through). 0 is risky because routine network events like ECMP or a route flap can shift TTL by 1 hop. The other rst_protection signals continue to apply regardless of this value, so loosening tolerance doesn't disable RST protection entirely.
fragmentation.strategy: Selects the TCP-level bypass technique b4 applies to matching outgoing packets. Options: tcp, ip, oob, tls, disorder, extsplit, firstbyte, combo, hybrid, or none. Each is a different way of breaking up the TLS ClientHello so DPI middleboxes can't match it as a single record. 'none' disables fragmentation for this set - packets pass through unmodified. Choosing the right strategy is ISP-dependent: what defeats one DPI engine fails on another. The discovery feature (separate b4 tab) tests combinations against the user's network and recommends one. When fragmentation.strategy_pool is non-empty, this fixed selection is ignored and the pool is sampled per packet instead.
fragmentation.reverse_order: For two-segment strategies (extsplit, firstbyte, tls, DNS fragmentation), sends segment 2 before segment 1 instead of the natural order. TCP sequence numbers correctly identify which segment is which, so the destination reassembles fine. Some DPI middleboxes refuse out-of-order segments rather than reassembling, which means a reversed order forces them to give up. Other DPI engines reassemble correctly regardless of order, in which case this toggle has no effect. Does not apply to multi-segment strategies (disorder, combo) which already reorder internally.
fragmentation.strategy_pool: List of strategies to randomly sample from on each matched packet. When non-empty, OVERRIDES fragmentation.strategy entirely - every packet picks a strategy uniformly at random from the pool. Useful when no single strategy works consistently, or when DPI fingerprints clients by repeated-strategy patterns and a random-per-packet selection avoids that fingerprint. Costs: harder to diagnose which strategy is actually helping (logs only show what was rolled for each packet), and a randomly-picked wrong strategy can produce intermittent failures. Empty (default) means use the single fixed strategy from the strategy field.
fragmentation.oob_position: Numeric position used by the 'oob' fragmentation strategy when constructing its modified packet. The min/max range form randomizes the value per packet to avoid a fixed pattern. 0 falls back to a strategy-internal default. Has no effect when the active strategy is anything other than 'oob' - including when 'oob' appears only inside the strategy_pool, in which case it's used only on packets the pool happens to roll. Tuning is ISP-dependent; the discovery feature finds working values automatically and manual tuning is rarely needed.
fragmentation.tlsrec_pos: Numeric position used by the 'tls' fragmentation strategy to split a single TLS record into two well-formed TLS records inside the ClientHello. Different from a TCP segment split: the TLS-layer framing itself is rewritten so the DPI engine sees two valid TLS records instead of one. The min/max range form randomizes the position per packet. 0 falls back to a strategy-internal default. Has no effect when the active strategy is not 'tls'. The discovery feature finds working values automatically; manual tuning is rarely needed.
fragmentation.combo.first_byte_split: One of the split-point options the 'combo' strategy can combine. When enabled, b4 inserts a split very early in the TCP payload, so the first byte of the TLS ClientHello travels alone before the rest. Designed to be combined with combo's other split options - using it alone is rarely effective. Has no effect outside the combo strategy (including when 'combo' appears only in fragmentation.strategy_pool, in which case it's used only on packets the pool happens to roll). Cost: an extra small TCP segment per matched connection - negligible bandwidth, marginal latency.
fragmentation.combo.extension_split: One of the split-point options the 'combo' strategy can combine. When enabled, b4 looks for a clean boundary inside the ClientHello's TLS extensions and inserts a split there, so the first portion of the extensions ends one segment and the rest (including SNI) begins another. Has no effect outside the combo strategy. May silently do nothing on a ClientHello that has no usable boundary - the strategy proceeds with its other splits. Cost: at most one extra segment per matched connection.
fragmentation.middle_sni: When enabled, b4 cuts the TLS SNI field (the server hostname) itself across multiple TCP segments instead of leaving it intact in one segment. Useful against DPI engines that need the full SNI string in a single read to match a blocklist. Applies to several strategies that process the ClientHello (combo, oob, disorder, others) - not just combo. Has no effect on strategies that don't look at SNI (e.g. plain tcp/ip splits) and on ClientHellos where the SNI position can't be located. Cost: more segments per connection.
fragmentation.combo.decoy_enabled: Combo-only feature: before emitting the real fragmented ClientHello, b4 first sends a fake decoy packet to the destination using a payload from the set's faking configuration. Goal: make the first thing a DPI engine sees on this connection look uninteresting, so its inspection state is in the wrong place when the real ClientHello arrives. Cost: one extra packet plus the decoy payload's bandwidth per matched connection. Has no effect when the set's faking configuration produces no usable decoy payload, or when the active strategy is not combo.
fragmentation.combo.shuffle_mode: Controls the order in which combo emits its built-up segments. 'full' randomizes the entire emit order. 'reverse' sends segments in reverse (last first). 'middle' keeps the first and last segments in place and shuffles whatever's between them - only does something when there are more than three segments. TCP sequence numbers ensure the destination reassembles correctly regardless of emit order. Picking the right mode is ISP-dependent: some DPI engines refuse out-of-order segments and any non-natural mode wins; others reassemble fine and the choice has no effect.
fragmentation.combo.first_delay_ms: Milliseconds to wait after emitting the first segment of a combo split, before continuing with the rest. The min/max range form randomizes the wait per packet. Goal: create a clear time gap so the first segment looks like a complete read to DPI engines with short read windows. Cost: every emitted ClientHello adds this much to TLS-handshake latency. Setting both min and max to 0 does NOT disable the wait - it falls back to a strategy-internal default. Has no effect when the active strategy is not combo.
fragmentation.combo.jitter_max_us: Maximum microseconds of random gap b4 inserts between consecutive segments AFTER the first one (the first uses first_delay_ms instead). Each gap is rolled randomly between 0 and this value. Goal: break repeating-timing patterns that DPI could use to identify a known bypass tool. The min/max range form randomizes the cap itself per connection. Cost: small added latency per emitted segment. Setting both min and max to 0 falls back to a strategy-internal default rather than disabling. Has no effect when the active strategy is not combo.
fragmentation.combo.fake_per_segment: When enabled, b4 emits fake (overlap) packets before EACH segment of a combo split, not just before the first one. Requires fragmentation.seq_overlap_pattern to be configured - without a pattern, this toggle does nothing regardless of state. Each fake-emit produces fake_per_seg_count copies (default 1, hard max 11). Goal: confuse DPI's stream-reassembly state at every segment boundary, not just the start. Cost: more emitted packets per matched connection - bandwidth multiplier plus added CPU. Has no effect when the active strategy is not combo.
fragmentation.seq_overlap_pattern: List of bytes used as the fake payload b4 emits before each real ClientHello segment when the active strategy supports it (combo and disorder). The fake segment shares TCP sequence space with the real one that follows but carries this byte pattern instead. UI presets: 'none' (empty - disables the trick), 'tls12'/'tls11'/'tls10' (mimic the start of TLS records of those versions), 'http_get' (mimics the start of an HTTP GET), 'zeros' (a single null byte), 'custom' (user-specified bytes). Goal: give DPI engines a plausible-looking 'first read' so their stream-reassembly state is set up against the fake before the real ClientHello arrives. Empty pattern means fake_per_segment and the related fake-emit features have nothing to emit - they become no-ops. Picking the right preset is ISP-dependent: which one (if any) helps depends on what the local DPI engine does with overlapping segment data. Discovery doesn't tune this - manual selection or empty are the typical choices.
fragmentation.disorder.shuffle_mode: Disorder-specific. Controls the order in which the disorder strategy emits its segments. 'full' randomizes the entire emit order. 'reverse' sends segments in reverse (last first). TCP sequence numbers ensure correct reassembly at the destination regardless of emit order. Note: disorder, unlike combo, does NOT have a 'middle' mode. Picking the right mode is ISP-dependent: some DPI engines refuse out-of-order segments (any non-natural mode wins), others reassemble correctly (the choice has no effect). Has no effect when the active strategy is not disorder.
fragmentation.disorder.jitter: min_jitter_us and max_jitter_us together bound the random microsecond gap b4 inserts between consecutive segments under the disorder strategy. Each gap is rolled randomly in [min, max]. Goal: break repeating-timing patterns DPI could use to identify a known bypass tool. IMPORTANT interaction: this microsecond jitter is ONLY used when tcp.seg2delay is 0. If seg2delay is non-zero (millisecond delay set), seg2delay takes over and these jitter bounds are ignored entirely. When both fields are 0 or invalid, b4 falls back to a strategy-internal default rather than disabling. If max_jitter_us is set lower than min_jitter_us, max gets bumped up automatically - the configured min is treated as the floor.
fragmentation.disorder.fake_per_segment: When enabled (disorder strategy), b4 emits fake overlap packets before EACH segment of the disorder split, not just before the first one. Requires fragmentation.seq_overlap_pattern to be configured - without a pattern, this toggle does nothing regardless of state. Each fake-emit produces fake_per_seg_count copies (default 1, hard max 11). Goal: confuse DPI's stream-reassembly state at every segment boundary, not just the start. Cost: more emitted packets per matched connection - bandwidth multiplier and added CPU. Has no effect when the active strategy is not disorder.
fragmentation.sni_position: Numeric byte position from the start of the TCP payload at which the 'tcp' and 'ip' fragmentation strategies cut the ClientHello. The min/max range form randomizes the cut per packet. 0 means no fixed cut (the strategy falls back to a small built-in position only if nothing else applies). Combined with middle_sni: when both are set AND the SNI is locatable, the strategy produces a 3-segment split - one cut at this fixed position plus another inside the SNI region. Used only by the tcp and ip strategies; has no effect under combo, disorder, oob, tls, extsplit, or firstbyte (each has its own split logic). Discovery autotunes this per ISP; manual tuning is rarely needed.
fragmentation.seq_overlap_length: Number of pattern bytes b4 prepends to one of the real fragmentation segments, with that segment's TCP sequence number shifted backwards by the same amount. Default 0 (off). Independent of fake_per_segment, which emits separate ghost packets; this one extends a real segment in place. Requires fragmentation.seq_overlap_pattern to be set (the same pattern provides the fill bytes); with no pattern this field is a no-op. Applies only to the combo and disorder strategies. In combo, the prepended bytes extend the lowest-seq segment into pre-data sequence territory. In disorder, they are prepended to the second seq-order segment and overlap the previous segment's tail in sequence space; if the second segment's start position is not larger than this value, the prepend is silently skipped. Picking the right value is ISP-dependent and discovery does not tune it; leave at 0 unless a specific value is known to work on the local DPI.
faking.sni: Master toggle for the fake-SNI feature. When enabled, b4 sends one or more fake TLS ClientHello packets BEFORE the real one on each matched connection. The fakes are crafted to be discarded by the real server (via the chosen strategy) but still seen by DPI, so DPI's per-connection state gets primed against the fake before the real ClientHello arrives. Has no effect unless sni_seq_length > 0 (number of fake packets to send). The strategy, sni_type, ttl, and sni_seq_length fields shape what the fakes look like and how the destination ignores them.
faking.strategy: How fake-SNI packets get IGNORED by the real server while still being seen by DPI. Six options: 'ttl' (fakes have a low TTL so they expire in transit), 'pastseq' (fakes claim a stale TCP sequence number that the server discards as already-acked), 'randseq' (fakes claim a random out-of-window sequence number), 'tcp_check' (fakes have a corrupted TCP checksum that the server's stack drops), 'md5sum' (fakes carry a TCP MD5 option the server doesn't expect), 'timestamp' (fakes carry an old TCP timestamp so the server treats them as replayed). Picking the right one is ISP- and path-dependent: some strategies work where others don't because of how the local DPI inspects, and how middleboxes/route-TTLs along the path treat low-TTL packets. Has no effect when faking.sni is off.
faking.sni_type: What payload the fake ClientHello carries. 'random' (random bytes - cheapest, often won't fool deep DPI), 'google'/'duckduckgo' (pre-baked ClientHellos to widely-allowed sites - DPI may treat them as legitimate traffic), 'file' (a user-uploaded captured ClientHello - see Settings → Payloads to manage captures), 'zeros' (all-zero payload), 'inverted' (real payload bit-inverted), 'domain' (b4 builds a fake ClientHello on the fly with a user-specified SNI from payload_domain). Choice depends on what DPI inspects: generic random bytes rarely survive content-aware DPI, named-site payloads work better against pattern-matching DPI.
tcp.syn_fake: Sends a fake SYN packet BEFORE the real SYN that opens the connection. The fake SYN looks like a normal connection attempt to DPI but is discarded by the real server (low TTL or other tricks similar to fake-SNI). Goal: prime DPI's per-flow state at connection setup, before any TLS payload is exchanged. Pairs with syn_fake_len (the fake's payload size, 0 = no payload) and syn_ttl. Useful when DPI decides whether to inspect a flow based on what it sees in the early SYN exchange.
faking.tcp_md5: Sends an extra fake SYN carrying the TCP MD5 signature option (RFC 2385) before the real handshake. Real servers without an MD5 key configured silently discard MD5-signed packets - the option is rare outside BGP. Some DPI engines accept the MD5-signed fake into their per-flow state because the option looks 'authentic', then discount subsequent unsigned packets as inconsistent. This option affects the connection-opening fake only; to put MD5 on the fake ClientHello itself use faking.md5_on_fake. Does not modify the real outgoing data.
faking.md5_on_fake: Puts the TCP MD5 signature option (RFC 2385) on the fake ClientHello itself, rather than on a separate fake SYN. The server discards the signed fake because it has no MD5 key configured, while DPI in the middle still reads it and takes its contents into the flow's state. This is the option byedpi exposes as -S, and it is usually paired with a low fake TTL and faking.fake_len_mode 'match' so the fake both dies in transit and covers exactly the bytes the real ClientHello occupies. Requires faking.sni.
faking.apply_ttl: Applies faking.ttl to the fake ClientHello regardless of which faking strategy is selected. Without it the TTL is only written to the fake ClientHello when faking.strategy is 'ttl', so a set could carry a TTL value while that fake still left at the full system TTL and reached the far end. Note that faking.ttl is read by the SYN fake paths under every strategy (as the fallback when tcp.syn_ttl is 0, and always for the MD5 fake SYN), so the value is never entirely inert - this option only governs the fake ClientHello. Turn it on to combine a low-TTL fake, which expires before the server, with a sequence or timestamp trick in the same set. The value is clamped below the real packet's TTL and never drops under 1.
faking.fake_len_mode: Controls how long the fake packet is. Default ('') emits the fake payload at whatever size it happens to be, which can be several times the size of the real ClientHello. 'match' sizes the fake to the real TLS payload, padding by repeating the payload or truncating it, and rewrites the TLS record length so the fake still parses as one complete record. A fake that does not cover the same byte range as the real data leaves a DPI that reassembles the connection an untouched copy of the real bytes to read, which is why byedpi always sizes its fake to the split it performs.
tcp.desync.mode: Sends a fake control packet (RST/FIN/ACK or combinations) crafted to make DPI think the connection is being torn down or has changed state, while the real connection continues. Modes: 'off' disables. 'rst' sends a fake RST. 'fin' sends a fake FIN. 'ack' sends a fake ACK. 'combo' sends RST+FIN+ACK. 'full' sends the strongest combination. Goal: trick DPI into dropping its per-flow inspection state for this connection; the real server is unaffected because the fakes are crafted to be discarded (low TTL/bad sequence/etc.). desync.ttl and desync.count tune the fakes' TTL and how many copies are sent. Cost: extra packets per matched connection.
tcp.desync.post_desync: When enabled, b4 sends an extra desync RST AFTER the fragmentation strategy finishes emitting the real ClientHello. Goal: tear down DPI's per-flow inspection state once the real data has been delivered, so DPI doesn't keep inspecting follow-up traffic on the same connection. Adds one extra packet per matched connection. Effective only when used together with an active fragmentation strategy; the post-desync packet is sent after fragmentation completes regardless of desync.mode.
tcp.win.mode: Manipulates the TCP receive-window field on emitted fake packets to confuse DPI engines that track flow state by window size. Modes: 'off' disables. 'zero' sends a fake zero-window probe before the real packet (DPI may treat the connection as paused/closed). 'random' sends multiple fakes with random window values drawn from tcp.win.values. 'oscillate' sends fakes with each value from tcp.win.values in order. 'escalate' uses an internal escalating sequence. The fakes are discarded by the real server (low TTL) but seen by DPI. Cost: 1 to N extra packets per matched connection depending on mode and the configured values list.
tcp.incoming.mode: Server-to-client bypass - what b4 does with INCOMING traffic from the server. Modes: 'off' disables. 'fake' injects a fake server response with corrupted contents so DPI updates its state to that fake; the real reply arriving later may be ignored by DPI. 'reset' injects an RST that closes DPI's idea of the connection while the real server's data continues to flow. 'fin' injects a FIN with similar effect. 'desync' injects malformed packets to break DPI's reassembly state. The min/max threshold fields bound the payload sizes at which this acts (so it doesn't trigger on every tiny ACK). Cost: at least one extra packet on matching incoming flows.
tcp.incoming.strategy: How the fake incoming packet is malformed so the LOCAL TCP stack discards it (preserving the real connection) while DPI still ingests it. 'badsum' corrupts the TCP checksum. 'badseq' offsets the sequence number out of the receive window. 'badack' offsets the ACK number. 'rand' picks one of the others at random. 'all' tries each in turn. Has no effect when tcp.incoming.mode is off. Which one works depends on whether DPI validates the same fields the local stack does - most DPI is more lax than a real TCP stack.
faking.sni_mutation.mode: Modifies the REAL TLS ClientHello before sending so DPI's pattern-matchers fail to recognize it. 'off' disables. 'random' applies a random mutation. 'grease' inserts GREASE-style padding into the cipher/extension lists. 'padding' adds a padding extension to inflate the ClientHello. 'fakeext' inserts non-standard fake extensions. 'fakesni' inserts a decoy SNI alongside the real one. 'advanced' stacks several mutations together. Some modes use extra tuning fields (grease_count, padding_size, fake_ext_count, fake_snis). Mutations are wire-compatible with real servers - TLS spec requires unknown extensions be ignored. Risk: very strict or buggy servers may reject mutated ClientHellos; if a site stops working after enabling a mutation mode, that's a likely cause.
system.web_server.mcp.token: Long-lived credential AI apps present to reach the MCP endpoint, sent as an 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' header. It exists because b4's web login tokens are browser session tokens: they live in memory and are destroyed on every restart or update, so an MCP client configured with one silently breaks. The MCP token is stored in the config file instead, so it survives restarts, and it can be regenerated independently without logging browser sessions out. When set, it is the ONLY accepted credential for /api/mcp - a web session token will not work there, and the token grants access to nothing else: presenting it on any other API route is rejected. When empty, MCP falls back to the web server's authentication (a token is required only if a username and password are set). It is compared in constant time. Generate one from the web UI rather than inventing a short string; the generated value is 32 random bytes as 64 hex characters. Because it is a bearer credential over plain HTTP unless TLS is configured, treat it like a password and prefer HTTPS when the port is reachable outside a trusted network.
system.web_server.mcp.allow_active_probe: Lets the MCP server make the router emit real traffic. Default false, and it is a SEPARATE permission from system.web_server.mcp.allow_writes: writing a setting and fetching a site are different acts, and neither implies the other. When off, b4_test_domain_now (fetch a domain once through b4 and once with b4 bypassed) and b4_find_bypass_strategy (a discovery run that brute-forces strategies until one loads the site) are not published at all, so a model sees no tool rather than a refusal; the server instructions still name this switch so it can tell the user what to turn on instead of concluding b4 cannot do it. It also gates the three b4_watchdog actions that cause a fetch: add puts a new host on the watchdog's timer, enable starts fetching every watched host on a schedule, and check re-tests one immediately. b4_watchdog action=status is never gated, because it only reports verdicts already recorded. What turning it on costs: a discovery run takes minutes to tens of minutes, installs its own firewall steering rules and a second packet queue for the duration, defers watchdog healing, and makes a firewall refresh wait up to five minutes. Only one run exists at a time and the watchdog's self-healing shares that runtime, so each blocks the other. Private, loopback, link-local, carrier-grade-NAT and multicast addresses are refused by every one of these tools, so the capability cannot be turned into a LAN scanner; a name that merely RESOLVES to such an address is reported as a sinkholed DNS answer, which is a censorship verdict rather than a refusal. Enabling the watchdog through this switch also lets b4 rewrite a strategy set on its own when a watched domain keeps failing, which is the one way an MCP session can change configuration later without another tool call.
system.web_server.mcp.allow_writes: Lets the MCP server change configuration, not just read it. Default false, and the read-only tools work regardless. When off, the tools that change configuration are not published at all, so a model sees no way to write rather than a refusal. When on, the writable surface is every scalar setting inside a strategy set - fragmentation, faking, TCP and UDP, DNS, escalation and routing - plus the MTProto and SOCKS5 subsystems and the logging settings. A set's target lists are NOT written through b4_set_config_value, which replaces a list wholesale: they belong to b4_edit_set_targets, which validates each entry and hands a domain over from whichever set already held it. Creating, duplicating, moving, resetting and deleting a set belong to b4_manage_set. This switch does not permit traffic: fetching a domain and running a discovery search are behind system.web_server.mcp.allow_active_probes, and so are the b4_watchdog actions that make the router fetch something (add, enable and check). system.logging.level accepts error, info, trace and debug, and debug is the most verbose of the four. The b4_list_writable_paths tool reports the exact paths with their types, current values and accepted values, so the model does not have to guess one. Refused however this is set: every credential, the web server settings, the MCP settings themselves, the packet capture engine (queue.mode and the TUN settings), the firewall backend, b4's packet marks, a set's id, the log directory and the geo file locations. Those last two are locations rather than contents: moving the log directory would silently stop file logging, and a wrong geo path would empty every geosite category at once. The dividing line is recoverability rather than sensitivity: a wrong value inside a set breaks some sites and can be seen and undone, while a wrong web-server port or capture engine can leave the machine unreachable with no way back in. Writable subtrees are named explicitly in the binary, so a setting added later is unwritable until someone opts it in. Writes go through the same validation, live-apply and firewall-refresh path as the web interface, so an invalid result is rejected and nothing is saved, and an accepted change takes effect immediately without a restart. Each write is snapshotted first, and b4_revert_last_change restores the previous configuration, walking back one change at a time; that history is in memory and is cleared when b4 restarts. The tools are marked destructive in MCP, so AI apps such as Claude Desktop and LM Studio prompt for approval before each call. Turning this on does not weaken authentication: MCP still follows the web server's auth setting.
system.web_server.mcp.enabled: Exposes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at /api/mcp on the same web-server port, so an external AI app (Claude Desktop, LM Studio, Cursor, Jan) can read b4's state and help diagnose problems. The exposed tools report status, config, strategy sets, domain coverage, recent connections, the log tail, metrics and diagnostics. They are read-only on their own; the tools that change anything (b4_set_config_value, b4_edit_set_targets, b4_manage_set and b4_revert_last_change) are not published until system.web_server.mcp.allow_writes is turned on as well, and even then they can only reach a short fixed allow-list. The tools that make the router emit traffic (b4_test_domain_now and b4_find_bypass_strategy) need system.web_server.mcp.allow_active_probes, a separate switch. The AI model runs entirely in the external app; b4 never contacts an AI provider for this and needs no API key, which is why it works on a headless router where the AI app runs on your laptop instead. Authentication: when system.web_server.mcp.token is set it is the only credential accepted here. When it is empty, MCP follows the web server, so requests need the usual Bearer token if a username and password are configured, and none at all if they are not. Leaving it open is a deliberate choice - an unauthenticated web UI already exposes far more, since the REST API can rewrite config and returns unredacted secrets, so gating MCP alone would buy nothing. Regardless of authentication, a browser request is accepted only when its Origin is b4's own address written as an IP address or localhost. Matching the Origin against the Host header would not stop DNS rebinding, because there the attacker owns the name and it appears in both headers; an attacker cannot, though, serve a page whose origin is an address they do not control. Reaching b4 from a browser by hostname needs that hostname in system.web_server.mcp.allowed_origins. Secrets are stripped from anything returned, since tool output may be forwarded to a third-party model: the web password and username, SOCKS5 credentials, MTProto secrets, the ipinfo token, the MCP token itself, and the proxy username and password a set carries for its upstream. b4_diagnostics is not secret but is identifying: it reports the hostname, every interface address and the live firewall ruleset. Costs nothing when disabled: no port is opened and no goroutines run.
dns.doh_url: Full https:// URL of an RFC 8484 DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint, e.g. https://xbox-dns.ru/dns-query. Default empty string. When non-empty and dns.enabled is true it OVERRIDES dns.target_dns entirely: both fields can be stored at once, every read site prefers the URL, and the IP is never dialled (the UI hides this by clearing the other field when you flip the resolver-type toggle). Validate rejects the config only when dns.enabled is true and the URL lacks the https:// prefix, so an http:// URL on a disabled set saves fine. b4 POSTs the wire-format query and retries once as a base64url GET only on HTTP 405 or 501; any other non-200 is a failure that hands over to the dns.strict logic. One shared http.Client serves every set, dialling with queue.mark, so the TLS handshake to the DoH host bypasses b4's own queue and gets NO bypass strategy. Footgun: the URL's hostname is resolved by the system resolver first, so a poisoned or blocked bootstrap disables DoH for the set, and dns.strict then decides what the client sees - a stale cached answer or a retry through the resolver it was originally addressing when false, SERVFAIL when true. A URL whose host is an IP literal avoids the dependency.
dns.enabled: Master switch for this set's DNS redirect; boolean, default false (config/config.go:95). Turning it on does nothing on its own: b4 only takes a query over when dns.enabled is true AND at least one of dns.doh_url or dns.target_dns is non-empty. Otherwise a matched query is logged dns-passthrough and forwarded UNCHANGED to whatever resolver the client already had. False does NOT mean b4 ignores DNS for the set: it still reads the reply on the way back, so host hints, routing IP-set population, ip_block_detect answer healing and the IPv4-fallback AAAA strip all still apply. dns.pins is checked BEFORE this flag, so pins answer even with dns.enabled false; pins are a map, and mcpDescribeKind has no reflect.Map case, so they never appear in b4_list_writable_paths and b4_set_config_value refuses them -- pins are editable only in the UI or the config file. This flag also gates infrastructure: the TCP-53 redirect into b4's listener is installed only if some enabled set passes the same enabled+resolver test, so a pins-only set gets no TCP DNS interception at all. Resolution is capped at 64 in flight across all sets and workers; past that a matched query is logged dns-overload and passed through.
dns.fragment_query: Boolean, default false. NOT an MTU or packet-size setting: when true b4 hand-builds the outgoing UDP query and splits it into exactly TWO IP fragments (IPv4 or IPv6) at a point inside the QNAME -- findDNSSplitPoint returns offset 12 + qnameLen/2, then the fragmenter rounds the first fragment's payload down to an 8-byte boundary -- so a DPI box that pattern-matches the domain name inside a query sees only half of it in the first fragment. The fragmenters hand back the tail fragment first, but sets ship with fragmentation.reverse_order true, which swaps them, so out of the box the offset-0 head fragment goes first and setting fragmentation.reverse_order false is what produces tail-first sending. That flag is set-wide rather than DNS-local: changing it to tune fragment order also re-orders every TCP and TLS segment this set splits. The gap between the two sends is udp.seg2delay / udp.seg2delay_max in milliseconds. Applies only to the plain-UDP path -- dns.target_dns and the non-strict fallback to the client's own resolver -- and never to dns.doh_url. Silently a no-op when the raw sender is missing, IPv6 is not ready, or the packet cannot be split: it falls back to an ordinary unfragmented write with no error and no log. Cost: many networks and middleboxes drop fragmented UDP outright, so the resolver stops answering and dns.strict then decides whether the client gets a stale answer or SERVFAIL.
dns.strict: Boolean, default false (zero value; not listed in DefaultSetConfig). Labelled 'Fail closed when the resolver is unreachable' and it reads as the safer choice, but what it does is DISABLE both recovery paths. With strict false, a failed lookup against dns.target_dns or dns.doh_url falls back first to b4's in-memory cache of the last good answer for that name (kept 1 hour, replayed with a 60-second TTL, 4096 entries), and if the cache is empty it re-asks the resolver the client was originally addressing and serves that. Three consecutive failures also take the resolver out of the path for 30 seconds, so a dead resolver costs one timeout instead of one per query; that health map is keyed by the resolver string and shared by every set using it. With strict true none of that runs: the fallback returns nothing and the client gets SERVFAIL, and the 30-second breaker is skipped too, so EVERY query still waits out system.dns.query_timeout_sec (5s default) against a resolver already known to be dead. escalate.dns_threshold still fires. Footgun: on a censored link the DoH host is itself a target, so strict takes every domain the set covers offline while the bypass underneath is still working.
dns.target_dns: Plain-DNS resolver for this set, written as a bare IP literal: no port, no hostname, no URL. Port 53 is hardcoded (ForwardOptions.Port defaults to 53 and nothing ever sets it). Default empty string. Read only when dns.enabled is true and dns.doh_url is EMPTY; a non-empty doh_url wins on every code path and this field is then never parsed. Nothing validates it at save time -- only doh_url is checked -- so a hostname, an ip:port or stray whitespace passes Validate, then fails net.ParseIP at packet time and the query is logged dns-bad-target and forwarded unchanged, which looks like the redirect silently doing nothing. b4 sends the query itself from a socket carrying queue.mark, and the nftables output chain accepts marked packets before the queue jump, so this set's fragmentation and faking strategies are NOT applied to it; dns.fragment_query is the only DPI evasion available on this path. TCP-53 queries that b4 intercepts are answered by forwarding to this same IP over UDP.
enabled: Per-set on/off switch, default true. False does not merely stop the bypass, it removes the set from everything at runtime: it is never added to the SNI/IP matcher, the startup expansion skips it, though every later config save re-expands all sets regardless, so once b4 has been written to a disabled set still costs its GeoSite/GeoIP memory, its tcp.dport_filter and udp.dport_filter ports never reach the firewall capture rules, its routing and TPROXY rules are not installed, its per-set MSS clamp is dropped, and host hints naming it are ignored. Escalation stops in both directions: an escalate.to pointing at a disabled set produces nothing, and live escalations onto it are pruned on the next config push - but the escalate.to link itself is KEPT (sanitizeEscalation only logs it at trace), so it resumes the moment the set is re-enabled. A disabled set still HOLDS its domain list: the pass that releases domains to the set being applied skips disabled sets, so its SNI entries survive another set claiming the same domain, they simply never compete for traffic. Footgun: nothing logs that a domain went unmatched because its set is off.
escalate.dns_threshold: How many unusable DNS answers for the same domain AND the same query type must be seen before that domain is switched to escalate.to. Default 2; 0 or negative resolves to 2 (ResolvedDNSThreshold), so 0 does not disable it. Unusable means an empty response, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED, any other non-zero rcode, or NOERROR for an A query that carries no address; an empty AAAA answer counts as GOOD because that is how an IPv4-only site answers, and question types other than A and AAAA are ignored entirely. The counter key is domain plus qtype (domain|a, domain|aaaa) so IPv4 and IPv6 lookups are counted separately, while the resulting escalation is stored per domain. A good answer of that query type clears that domain+qtype counter and leaves the other type's count untouched. The counting window is a HARDCODED 120 seconds - escalate.rst_window_sec does not apply here. 1 escalates on the first bad answer. It is the only trigger that can repair the request that tripped it, and only when the backup set is able to answer: it needs a DNS pin for that name, or dns.enabled with a dns.target_dns or dns.doh_url. Otherwise the switch is recorded and the original failure still reaches the client. It fires both on b4's own DNS redirect path and on passively observed DNS responses.
escalate.rst_threshold: How many incoming RSTs that b4 judges FORGED, for the same hostname, must arrive inside escalate.rst_window_sec before that host is switched to escalate.to. Default 3; 0 or any negative value resolves back to 3 (ResolvedRstThreshold), so 0 does not disable the trigger - only an empty escalate.to does. Only RSTs that connStateTracker.CheckRST flags as injected are counted (RST before any server response, TCP options stripped relative to the server's, bare RST without ACK, TTL differing from the server's by more than tcp.rst_protection.ttl_tolerance, or a repeat RST on the same connection). Counting is keyed by hostname, so the connection must have a cached SNI; RSTs on connections with no known host are never counted. 1 escalates on the very first forged RST. When the threshold trips the counter entry is DELETED, so the next round starts from zero. This trigger runs even with tcp.rst_protection.enabled false - the RST is then counted but not dropped, so the connection that tripped it is already lost; enabling RST protection is what keeps the current page alive while b4 decides.
escalate.rst_window_sec: Seconds within which the forged RSTs counted by escalate.rst_threshold must arrive. Default 30; 0 or negative resolves to 30, both in ResolvedRstWindow and again in RecordRSTKill, so it can never be zero at runtime. It is NOT a rolling window: the window starts at the first counted RST for that host, and the first RST arriving after firstAt+window resets the counter to 1 and opens a fresh window, so a host being reset once every 31 seconds with the default settings never escalates. The window in force is captured into the counter entry when it is created, so a live change to this value only affects hosts whose counting starts afterwards. It applies ONLY to the forged-RST trigger: the DNS trigger uses a hardcoded 120-second window that no setting exposes, and the stall trigger has no window at all (its per-connection ClientHello entries are pruned after 120 seconds). Larger values make escalation more eager by letting older resets keep counting.
escalate.stall_threshold: How many ClientHello packets b4 must see on the SAME connection (same source IP/port to destination IP/port) before the host is switched to escalate.to. Because a stalled handshake shows up as the client retransmitting its ClientHello, the default 3 means the original plus two retransmits. Default 3; 0 or negative resolves to 3 (ResolvedStallThreshold), so 0 does not disable the trigger. NEVER set it to 1 - the first ClientHello of every matched TLS connection already counts as 1, so 1 escalates every connection immediately. When the trigger fires b4 DROPS the ClientHello that tripped it, deliberately killing that connection so the client's retry lands on the backup set. The per-connection counter is only kept while the set matches, the hostname is known, the port is a configured TCP port and either escalate.to is set or tcp.ip_block_detect.enabled is on; entries are pruned after 120 seconds. escalate.stall_timeout_ms is a second, independent path to the same trigger and can fire before this count is reached.
escalate.stall_timeout_ms: Milliseconds; the age-based half of the stalled-handshake trigger. escalateOnStall switches the host when the ClientHello count reaches escalate.stall_threshold OR when the count is greater than 1 AND more than stall_timeout_ms has passed since the FIRST ClientHello of that connection. It is therefore not a timer: the check only runs when another ClientHello packet arrives, so a connection that sends one ClientHello and then goes silent forever never trips it, no matter how long it waits. Default 3000 (3 seconds); 0 or negative resolves to 3000 (ResolvedStallTimeout), so 0 does not disable it. The smaller it is, the more often the age path wins over escalate.stall_threshold; whatever the value, it can never fire before the second ClientHello of a connection. Unrelated to tcp.ip_block_detect.timeout_ms, which times SYN health, not handshakes. Firing this trigger drops the ClientHello that tripped it.
escalate.to: The ID of the set traffic is handed to when this set keeps failing for a host - the target set's `id` field, NOT its name. Empty (the default) means escalation is off: EscalateConfig.Active() is exactly `To != ""` and gates every trigger, so clearing it stops NEW escalations - but it does not release hosts already escalated, which keep using the backup set until escalate.ttl_sec expires, the counters are reset from the interface, or a reload finds the target set deleted or disabled. On every save Validate() runs sanitizeEscalation, which SILENTLY REWRITES bad values and still lets the save succeed with no validation error: a value that is not the id of an existing set is cleared with a warning, a self-reference is cleared, and a chain that closes a loop has its last link cleared. So setting a set NAME here looks accepted and simply disables escalation. A link to a DISABLED set is kept (trace-logged only) and sits idle until that set is enabled again. Chains A->B->C are walked per host up to 8 hops (MaxEscalationHops). Costs of turning it on: ClientHello stall tracking, SYN health probing and forged-RST classification all start running for this set even when tcp.ip_block_detect and tcp.rst_protection are off, and in TUN mode it forces reply-direction packet capture.
escalate.ttl_sec: Seconds a host stays pinned to the escalated set before b4 falls back to this set and starts detecting again. Default 3600 (one hour); 0 or negative resolves to 3600 both in ResolvedTTL and again in SetEscalation. The UI shows this control in MINUTES and writes minutes*60, so the stored value is always seconds. The clock starts when the switch happens and is NEVER refreshed by continued successful use of the backup - after ttl_sec the pin expires and the host silently returns to the original set, so the whole failure cycle has to repeat before it switches again. The TTL applied is the one from the set that DID the escalating, not from escalate.to's own config, so in a chain A->B->C the A->B pin uses A's ttl_sec and the later B->C pin uses B's, and every new hop restarts the clock from scratch. Expiry is lazy: lookups treat an expired entry as absent and a background Cleanup deletes it. A config reload also drops any pin whose target set has been deleted or disabled, and the Dashboard's Reset Stats clears all pins at once.
mss_clamp.enabled: Turns on a per-set MSS clamp, which is a FIREWALL rule (nftables `tcp option maxseg size set` / iptables `TCPMSS`) and not part of b4's packet-mangling path. Default false. It rewrites the MSS option on TCP SYN and SYN-ACK for port 443 ONLY: tcp.dport_filter does not widen it. Because MSS is written before any ClientHello exists, it can only be scoped by targets.ip, targets.geoip_categories or included targets.source_devices, and Validate REJECTS the whole config (mss_clamp_scope_required) when the set has none of those; targets.source_devices_exclude makes devices stop counting as scope. The set's own enabled must be true and mss_clamp.size must be > 0 or the entry is dropped silently. A per-set clamp overrides queue.devices[].mss_clamp and the global queue.mss_clamp for the connections it covers, because its rule is emitted so it matches last. Changes reapply live through the MSS fingerprint, no restart. Footguns: b4's rule monitor only re-verifies global and per-device clamps, so a per-set rule flushed by another firewall tool stays gone until the next tables refresh, and on the iptables backend the IP-scoped rules are skipped with a warning when the ipset binary is missing.
mss_clamp.size: MSS value in BYTES written into the TCP MSS option of matched SYN and SYN-ACK packets, not a percentage and not a segment count. The stored default is 0, and 0 does NOT mean off: while mss_clamp.enabled is true, Validate rewrites <=0 to 88, raises 1-9 to 10, and lowers anything above 1460 to 1460, so the effective default is 88 (the value the UI also fills in when the switch is flipped on, and the usual Smart-TV/YouTube workaround). While mss_clamp.enabled is false the field is left exactly as written and CollectSetMSSClamps additionally requires Size > 0, so an unsupplied size only becomes 88 once the clamp is enabled and the config revalidated. The global queue.mss_clamp.size ships as 88 as well but is rewritten differently: while queue.mss_clamp.enabled is true, 0 is raised to 10 rather than 88, so writing 0 there installs a 10-byte MSS on every matched connection on the router instead of disabling anything - only queue.mss_clamp.enabled false disables it. The per-device MSS clamp is the one field in this family where 0 really does mean off. Cost: a small MSS multiplies packet count and per-packet header overhead on every connection the set covers, and at the 10-byte floor almost the whole segment is headers.
name: Free-text display label for the set, default empty. Nothing in the packet path matches on it - it exists for logs, warnings and the UI. It doubles as an address: MCP set paths resolve the bracket by id OR name, case-insensitively, so sets[video].tcp.seg2delay works, and b4_get_set accepts either; the id field itself carries mcp:"deny" and can never be written, so the name is the only human-writable handle on a set. BUT escalate.to takes the set ID (a UUID) SPECIFICALLY: sanitizeEscalation looks its value up in a map keyed by Id alone and CLEARS it with a warning when it does not match, so putting a name there silently destroys the escalation chain at the next validate. Names are not required to be unique and nothing enforces it; lookup returns the first match in config order, so two sets sharing a name make the later one unaddressable by name. Renaming is safe for escalate.to, which stores the UUID, but breaks every saved MCP path that used the old name.
routing.block_action: Which of two literal strings a block-mode set uses, 'drop' or 'reject'; default 'reject'. NormalizeBlockAction maps ANY value that is not exactly 'drop' - a typo, or a legacy 'reject-tcp-reset' - to 'reject', and it is applied only when routing.mode is 'block'. 'reject' emits two filter-hook rules per family, 'reject with tcp reset' for TCP and 'reject with icmpx type port-unreachable' for everything else (iptables: REJECT --reject-with tcp-reset / icmp-port-unreachable / icmp6-port-unreachable), and additionally makes the NFQUEUE worker send a RST to the client on a matched ClientHello and an ICMP unreachable on matched QUIC. 'drop' emits a plain 'drop' and stays silent, so clients hang until they time out. The part a model gets wrong: this also changes DNS, but for UDP port 53 only. Under 'reject' b4 sinkholes a matched query with an NXDOMAIN answer; under 'drop' the query is discarded and the client waits out its own timeout. DNS over TCP never reads this setting and is answered NXDOMAIN for any block-mode set, 'drop' included.
routing.egress_interface: Name of the kernel network interface matched traffic leaves through in mode 'interface' - wg0, tun0, ppp0, a LAN bridge. Default empty, and empty is NOT 'use the default route': in interface mode it makes b4 install NO rule for the set and skip it on every sync, so routing reads as enabled while doing nothing. Read only in mode 'interface'; 'proxy', 'mtproto-ws' and 'block' never look at it. Validation strips every character outside [A-Za-z0-9._-], so a name pasted with a space or a colon is silently truncated instead of rejected. The interface name joined with routing.egress_ip is the key b4 hashes to auto-assign the set's fwmark (0x100-0x7EFF) and routing table (100-249), so two sets with the same pair share one mark and one table. If the interface is absent when rules are built, the ip rule is still installed and the default route is deferred until the link appears.
routing.egress_ip: Source address stamped on this set's outgoing packets in place of the interface's own: it replaces the set's POSTROUTING masquerade with 'snat to <ip>' pinned to oifname routing.egress_interface. Default empty, which means masquerade. Validation rewrites this field aggressively: an unspecified, loopback or multicast address is a hard config error; any routing.mode other than 'interface' clears it with a warning; an empty routing.egress_interface clears it with a warning. b4 ARP-probes the address (arping -D), adds it to the interface as /32 or /128, and removes it again when the last set stops using it; if another host answers, the add fails, or the address is simply not on the interface when rules are built, b4 falls back to masquerade and logs it. Only the matching family is rewritten - an IPv4 value leaves the set's IPv6 traffic masqueraded. The real footgun is upstream: b4 only stamps the source, so a router with strict rp_filter and no route back for that address drops everything while b4's rules still look correct.
routing.enabled: Master switch for this set's traffic routing; default false. Turning it on is not sufficient on its own: b4 installs rules only when the set itself is enabled AND the set has at least one IP or domain target, because every rule b4 writes matches a DESTINATION - a set with only source devices or only a port filter steers nothing, b4 skips it during sync and logs that no rule was installed. Mode 'interface' additionally requires a non-empty routing.egress_interface, and mode 'proxy' a valid upstream port, or the set is skipped silently. Enabling it also changes the DPI-bypass path: for routing.mode 'proxy' and 'mtproto-ws' the NFQUEUE worker accepts matched packets unmodified, so faking, fragmentation and desync are DISABLED for that traffic and the upstream alone is responsible for getting through. It also starts feeding addresses from DNS answers b4 observes into the set's nftables set/ipset.
routing.ip_ttl_seconds: Lifetime in SECONDS of one dynamically learned address inside the set's nftables set - an 'nft element ... timeout Ns' in the companion '<name>_d' set, which is the timeout-flagged half of the pair b4 creates - or the ipset entry timeout on the iptables backend. Default 3600; any value <= 0 is rewritten to 3600 by validation and again at every runtime use site, so 0 does NOT mean 'never expire'. It is not the DNS record's TTL: the A/AAAA TTL in the observed response is ignored and this fixed value is used instead. It applies only to addresses b4 learns (DNS answers it sees, pre-resolution, learned hostnames); IPs listed in the set's targets are added with timeout 0 into the interval set and are PERMANENT, contrary to what docs/docs/sets/routing.md claims. Background re-resolution runs at ip_ttl_seconds/2 but never faster than 5 minutes, so a value below 600 leaves a window where entries have already expired and nothing has refreshed them, and routing for that domain resumes only on the client's next DNS query.
routing.mode: One of four literal strings deciding what the kernel does with a matched packet. 'interface' (the default, and what an empty string is silently rewritten to) marks the packet with an auto-assigned fwmark in b4's own prerouting and output chains (table inet b4_route on the nftables backend, table mangle only on the iptables one, so do not send anyone to iptables -t mangle -S on an nft box), an ip rule sends that mark to a private routing table whose default route points at routing.egress_interface, and a postrouting nat rule masquerades or SNATs it. 'proxy' TPROXYs matched TCP into a per-set transparent listener on port 13000+(mark%50000), which opens a SOCKS5 CONNECT to the upstream and relays bytes. 'mtproto-ws' uses the same TPROXY diversion but bridges the session over Telegram's WebSocket edge using the shared Settings->MTProto upstream, so routing.upstream.host/port are never dialed. 'block' installs filter-hook rules only (see routing.block_action) and needs no egress and no listener. An unrecognized value is a HARD validation failure that rejects the whole config, not a silent fallback to 'interface'.
routing.router_traffic: One of three literal strings - 'auto' (default), 'include', 'exclude' - deciding whether the set's OUTPUT-chain rules also mark packets the router itself originates, so its own connections to the set's destinations leave through routing.egress_interface. Read only in mode 'interface'. A set that already carries routing.source_interfaces or targets.source_devices ignores this field and never marks router traffic, because that traffic arrives from no interface and no device. 'auto' includes router traffic unless the egress interface is a TUN/TAP device driven by a userspace program (detected by /sys/class/net/<iface>/tun_flags), in which case it excludes it and logs why: a proxy such as Xray or sing-box with a TUN inbound answers a connection by opening its own from this host to the same address, that address is in the set, so b4 marks the new connection and routes it straight back into the same TUN. Every turn is a fresh 5-tuple, so nothing dedupes it, and the box runs out of memory in minutes. 'include' forces the old behaviour and is right for a second WAN or a WireGuard uplink; b4 warns if it is used on a userspace TUN and installs a rate guard ahead of the marking (nft 'ct state new limit rate over 200/second return', iptables hashlimit) so a loop is capped rather than unbounded. 'exclude' never marks router traffic. Independent of the injected-packet rule, which always stays: the packets b4 reinjects for a set are locally generated, and OUTPUT is the only hook where they can regain the set's mark.
routing.kill_switch: Boolean, default false, read only in mode 'interface'. Off, if routing.egress_interface goes down the kernel drops the default route b4 put in the set's routing table, the fwmark rule then matches a table with nothing in it, and the lookup falls through to the main table - so the set's traffic silently leaves by the normal uplink instead of the tunnel, unprotected and with the box's real address. On, b4 also installs 'blackhole default metric 4096' in that table beside the real default at metric 0. While the interface is up the metric-0 route wins and nothing changes; when it disappears the blackhole is what remains, and the set's traffic is dropped instead of leaking. It is added and removed by the same code that maintains the ip rule, so it comes back on a link event and goes away with the rest of the table when the set stops routing. It holds only traffic this set matched: everything else keeps using the main table normally. Ignored, with a warning, in modes 'proxy', 'mtproto-ws' and 'block', which terminate the connection instead of steering it at an interface.
routing.source_interfaces: List of INGRESS interface names; each becomes an 'iifname "x"' qualifier (iptables '-i x') on the set's marking, TPROXY and block rules, so it filters which arriving traffic is offered to the rule - it never selects a destination and cannot route anything on its own. Default empty, and empty means no iifname qualifier at all: a single rule matching traffic arriving on any interface, including traffic the router itself originates. Names are character-sanitized to [A-Za-z0-9._-] on save, then trimmed, de-duplicated and sorted before rules are built. The footgun: a NON-EMPTY list makes the set source-scoped, which deletes its OUTPUT-chain rules entirely, so anything the router itself originates (curl on the box, its updater, its own resolver) is no longer routed, proxied or blocked by this set - that traffic arrives on no interface. Listing source devices under targets has the same source-scoping effect. In interface mode b4 also orders source-scoped sets' chain jumps ahead of unscoped ones.
routing.upstream.fail_open: Decides what a proxy-mode listener does when the SOCKS5 dial to the upstream fails (15s connect timeout for TCP, 10s for a UDP session). Default false: b4 closes the client connection and the request fails visibly, so nothing leaks direct. True: b4 opens a plain direct connection to the ORIGINAL destination, carrying b4's self-dial bypass mark so the OUTPUT rule does not re-divert it into a loop. The upstream endpoint itself (routing.upstream.host and .port) is not writable here and is configured in the web interface. Read only in mode 'proxy' - mode 'mtproto-ws' NEVER consults this flag and always falls open, first through a WebSocket worker and then to a direct dial. Changing it restarts the set's tproxy listener. Cost: fail-open exposes the destination to the ISP exactly when the proxy is down, which in whitelist-blocking regions converts a clear, diagnosable failure into a slow one that also defeats the point of routing through the proxy.
routing.upstream.udp: Also tunnels matched UDP through the upstream using SOCKS5 UDP ASSOCIATE, on top of TCP; default false. Only proxy-mode sets read it: validation forces it to false with a warning when routing.mode is 'mtproto-ws' (that bridge carries TCP only, and diverted UDP would land on a port with no listener and be dropped), and modes 'interface' and 'block' never look at it. Turning it on adds udp TPROXY rules alongside the tcp ones and starts a transparent UDP listener; if the upstream does not actually implement UDP ASSOCIATE, what happens next is decided by routing.upstream.fail_open: with it false every matched UDP datagram including QUIC is dropped and b4 warns once naming the set and the upstream, with it true b4 falls back to a direct marked UDP dial to the original destination, so the traffic leaves in the clear around the proxy instead of being blocked. Leaving it OFF is not passive: b4 then installs a per-family rule rejecting matched UDP destination port 443 with ICMP port-unreachable, so browsers abandon HTTP/3 and fall back to TCP through the proxy instead of reaching the destination directly over QUIC and bypassing routing entirely.
routing.upstream.use_domain: When b4 already knows a domain for the destination IP, it sends that domain in the SOCKS5 CONNECT request as ATYP 0x03 instead of the raw ATYP 0x01/0x04 address, so the upstream resolves the name itself and can pick a geographically correct server. Default TRUE - the only field under routing.upstream that defaults to on. The domain comes from b4's learned-IP table (the SNI suffix set), so it is present only for addresses b4 has already tied to a matched hostname; with no mapping the raw IP is sent and the setting is a no-op for that connection. TCP only: the UDP relay always sends the destination IP, and mode 'mtproto-ws' returns before the domain lookup ever runs. Changing it restarts the set's listener. Cost: if the IP-to-domain mapping is stale or an IP is shared by a CDN, the upstream is asked to connect somewhere other than the client asked for, and the upstream resolver's failures become connection failures.
system.logging.directory: Base folder for b4's log FILES, and empty disables file logging entirely rather than falling back anywhere. Exactly two files live here and they are not two verbosities of the same stream. errors.log holds ERROR lines ONLY: log.Errorf writes it regardless of system.logging.level, and Warnf, Infof, Tracef and Debugf never reach it at all, so raising the level adds nothing to this file and an empty errors.log means no errors were recorded, not that b4 was quiet. Each line is fsynced, so it survives a crash or a kill, and an 'error log opened pid=N' banner marks every restart. update.log is different in kind: it is the stdout and stderr of the installer, captured only when an update is started from the WEB INTERFACE, plus a few [HANDLER] lines b4 adds around it; an update run over SSH writes nothing here. It is the only record of what an update did, and nothing else in b4 exposes it: there is no REST endpoint and no UI view, so b4_logs_tail with file=update is the only way to read it without shell access. Both roll over at 1 MiB to a single .1 companion and the older file is dropped on the next roll, so evidence older than two files is gone. The verbose stream system.logging.level controls is NOT written to any file: it goes to the console, the journal and the web interface's live log view. The path itself is refused over MCP because moving it silently stops file logging, while reading either file is always allowed.
system.logging.instaflush: Boolean, default TRUE - despite reading like an opt-in optimisation, unbuffered logging is the shipped behaviour. True writes every log line straight through to the writers. False routes lines through a 16 KB bufio.Writer that a background ticker flushes every 2 seconds, so false is the throughput mode and it is the one that costs data: up to 2 seconds or 16 KB of lines are lost if b4 crashes or is killed, and the web UI's live log stream lags by the same amount. READ ONLY AT STARTUP, exactly like system.logging.syslog: log.Init receives it from initLogging and log.SetInstaflush is never called from outside the log package, so a change is persisted but needs a b4 restart to take effect. Only the fsynced errors.log copy is unaffected, and only while file logging is on (system.logging.directory non-empty): the console and web-UI copy of an error line goes through the same buffer, so with instaflush false error lines lag by the same 2 seconds and can be lost from stderr on a crash.
system.logging.level: Integer verbosity stored in the config file, and the numbering is NOT the usual one: error=0, info=1, trace=2, debug=3, so DEBUG IS THE MOST VERBOSE and trace sits between info and debug. Every call site tests CurLevel >= wanted, so each level includes everything numerically below it. Default is 1 (info). Errorf ignores the level entirely, so errors always print and always reach errors.log; Warnf only needs level >= 0. -1 means silent and is reachable from the --verbose silent CLI flag or by hand-editing the config file, since nothing range-checks the field; the web UI and MCP offer 0-3 only, and MCP additionally accepts the names error, info, trace and debug for those numbers. Validate does not range-check the field: a value above 3 logs everything while Level.String() misreports it as 'silent'. Applied live via log.SetLevel on any config write, including MCP writes, with no restart. Cost: trace and debug emit per-packet and per-rule detail and are heavy on a busy router.
system.logging.syslog: Boolean, default false. When true, b4 opens a syslog connection at startup (LOG_INFO | LOG_DAEMON, tag 'b4') and ADDS it as an extra writer alongside stderr - it does not replace console or journal output, and every line is emitted at LOG_INFO priority regardless of its b4 level. READ ONLY AT STARTUP: initLogging runs exactly once from main, and nothing calls EnableSyslog or AttachSyslog afterwards, so toggling this in the UI or over MCP persists the value and changes nothing until b4 is restarted; there is no detach path either, so once attached the writer stays for the life of the process. If syslog.New fails, b4 logs a warning and rewrites the in-memory field back to false, leaving the running configuration disagreeing with the file on disk. system.logging.level filters before the writers, so syslog receives exactly the console lines and there is no separate syslog verbosity.
targets.domain_only: Boolean, default false. When true it stops b4 from LEARNING destination addresses from this set's domains. Normally an SNI match records the destination IP in a ten-minute learned-IP cache, so later connections to that address match the set again even with no SNI to read (session resumption, ECH, plain TCP); with domain_only that learning is skipped and any pre-existing learned entry is refused, so only a readable SNI or DNS name can match. It also stops routing from adding DNS-resolved and SNI-resolved addresses to the set's nftables sets, while explicit targets.ip and targets.geoip_categories entries are still routed normally. Use it for shared CDN addresses where a neighbouring domain on the same IP needs a different set. Validate rejects nothing here; it only warns when domain_only is combined with routing.enabled and domain targets, because the addresses behind those domains will not be steered.
targets.geoip_categories: List of GeoIP category tags (country codes, ASNs) read from the .dat file named by system.geo.ipdat_path and expanded into the set's IP list, ahead of the manual targets.ip entries. Tags are lowercased and compared to the file's tags directly: unlike targets.geosite_categories there is NO @attr handling here, so cn@something matches nothing at all. An unknown category is skipped SILENTLY, contributing zero addresses with no error; Validate rejects only the separate case where system.geo.ipdat_path is empty. Expansion runs at daemon start and on every set save, and the resulting prefixes are loaded both into the in-process matcher and, when routing is on, into the set's nftables sets, so a whole-country category becomes thousands of nft elements. Default is empty.
targets.geosite_categories: List of category tags pulled from the geosite .dat file named by system.geo.sitedat_path and expanded into the set's domain list, ahead of targets.sni_domains. Expansion happens once at daemon start and on every set save, not per packet. Tag comparison is case-insensitive. An @attr suffix is PARSED AND DISCARDED: google@ads loads the whole google category, exactly as plain google would, because only the part before the @ is used as the tag. An unknown or misspelled category is skipped SILENTLY at expansion time, contributing zero domains with no error; Validate rejects only the separate case where system.geo.sitedat_path is empty, and a configured-but-missing file logs an error and yields nothing. Geosite full: and keyword: record kinds are flattened into plain suffix entries, so a keyword record becomes a suffix match rather than a substring match; only regex records keep a regexp: prefix. Default is empty.
targets.ip: List of destination IP addresses and CIDR ranges the set matches. The JSON key is singular (ip) but the value is ALWAYS an array. A bare address is widened to /32 for IPv4 and /128 for IPv6; anything net.ParseIP or net.ParseCIDR rejects is dropped SILENTLY when the matcher and the nftables routing sets are built, and nothing in Validate reports it. IP targets are evaluated on the very first packet of a connection, so they are the only target type that can catch a TCP SYN before any SNI exists, which is why per-set MSS clamping accepts only targets.ip, targets.geoip_categories or an included targets.source_devices as scope. When several sets cover the same address a set scoped to the source device wins first, then the LONGEST PREFIX, and list position only breaks ties between equally specific prefixes - so a device-scoped set holding 10.0.0.0/8 beats an unscoped set holding 10.1.2.3/32. The web interface's 'Match any IP address' switch writes 0.0.0.0/0, and adds ::/0 only when IPv6 is enabled in the core settings. Default is empty. Unlike learned addresses, these entries are still routed when targets.domain_only is on.
targets.ip_version: String filter selecting the IP version of the packet: "4", "6", or empty (the DEFAULT) for any. Like targets.tls this is a PREFERENCE, NOT A HARD FILTER: an exact-version set wins when one exists, but if no candidate matches the packet's version the matcher retries with the version ignored and every configured filter is then treated as satisfied, so a lone set with ip_version "4" still matches an IPv6 packet. Any other string, including the plausible-looking "ipv4" and "v6", makes the set match NOTHING: the invalid-value branch returns false and that survives the ignore-version retry. The selector is hidden in the web interface unless both queue.ipv4 and queue.ipv6 are enabled or the field is already non-empty, so a stale invalid value can sit in the config with no visible control to clear it.
targets.sni_domains: List of domain entries this set matches, tested against the SNI in a TLS or QUIC ClientHello and against DNS query names. Exactly two forms are accepted: a bare name, which matches that name AND every subdomain of it at a label boundary (example.com covers www.example.com but not notexample.com), and a regexp: prefix, whose pattern is compiled with Go's regexp and matched UNANCHORED, so regexp:example\.com also hits notexample.commercial.net. There is no wildcard syntax and no full:/keyword: prefix: *.example.com is stored verbatim and matches NOTHING; the web interface rewrites it to example.com and shows a notice saying so, while a raw config edit, an API PUT or an MCP write stores it exactly as typed and it then matches nothing. Entries are lowercased, trimmed and stripped of a trailing dot when the matcher is built. Literal entries are looked up before any regexp across every enabled set, so a regexp:.* catch-all never takes a name another set lists literally. Adding a domain through the interface's Add-to-set action, discovery, or a byedpi import REMOVES that entry from every other ENABLED set; editing this list in the set editor or writing it through the API does not, and a duplicate then resolves to the first enabled set in list order. Default is empty, which means the set matches no domain unless targets.geosite_categories supplies some.
targets.source_devices: List of MAC addresses that narrows the set to traffic originating from those LAN devices; empty (the default) means every source matches. The values are ALWAYS MACs, never IP addresses: a device added manually has no MAC on the wire, so b4 stores the synthetic MAC 02:B4:<four hex octets of its IP> and the DHCP/ARP layer maps that IP back to it. Comparison is case-insensitive. Traffic the router itself originates has NO source MAC, so it never matches a set with a non-empty list here unless targets.source_devices_exclude is set. Among sets listing the SAME domain, a device-scoped set is preferred over an unscoped one whatever their positions in the sets list; but there is no fallback across different entries, so if a device-scoped set owns the more specific entry (www.example.com) and the packet's device does not match, the broader entry (example.com) in another set is NOT tried and nothing matches at all. Source devices narrow who a set applies to, they never select traffic on their own: a routing set whose only target is a source device steers nothing and b4 installs no rule for it.
targets.source_devices_exclude: Boolean that inverts targets.source_devices from an include list into an exclude list: with it true, the set applies to every source EXCEPT the listed MACs. Default false. It has no effect at all when targets.source_devices is empty, because the matcher returns 'matches' immediately for an empty list whatever this flag says. The inversion also changes unknown-source traffic: a packet with no resolvable source MAC, which includes everything the router itself originates, does not match under an include list but DOES match under an exclude list. An exclude list is not counted as source SCOPE, and the two consequences pull in opposite directions. Per-set MSS clamping fails validation with mss_clamp_scope_required - a blocking error that rejects the whole save - unless the set also has IP, GeoIP or INCLUDED device targets. Routing goes the other way: because the set is not source-scoped it KEEPS its output-chain rules, so it starts steering traffic the router itself originates. Per-device rules are installed either way; for an exclude list they are negative return rules for the listed devices.
targets.tls: String filter on the client's maximum offered TLS version. Empty (the DEFAULT) means any version. "1.0", "1.1", "1.2" and "1.3" resolve to wire codes; the web interface offers only "", "1.2" and "1.3", and MCP writes accept only those three. For SNI matching this is a PREFERENCE, NOT A HARD FILTER: when no candidate set matches the observed version the matcher retries with the version ignored, and that pass treats every configured filter as satisfied, so a lone set with tls "1.2" still matches a TLS 1.3 ClientHello. It only decides between several sets covering the same domain. For a set matched by IP, port or learned IP the filter IS enforced once a ClientHello has actually been parsed, and the match is cleared on disagreement. Any string outside the four known values makes the set match NOTHING - not by domain, and not by IP or GeoIP either, because the version check fails even on the retry pass. Only port-only sets and addresses already learned escape it. QUIC is always evaluated as TLS 1.3.
