tcp.incoming.max: Upper bound, in KILOBYTES, of the incoming-byte threshold whose lower bound is tcp.incoming.min; b4 draws min + rand(0..max-min) KB once per connection and again after each injection. Default 14, the same as the default min, so out of the box the threshold is a fixed 14 KB. 0 means USE tcp.incoming.min, NOT 'no maximum': max == 0 or max < min is rewritten to min at runtime, and if min is also 0 or negative both become 14. Ignored entirely when tcp.incoming.mode is 'fake', which never consults a threshold. Randomizing is worth it when DPI fingerprints an injection that always lands at the same offset in the stream; the UI caps it at 50 KB, and a threshold beyond what the queue.tcp_conn_bytes_limit window delivers simply never fires.
tcp.incoming.min: Lower bound, in KILOBYTES (the value is multiplied by 1024), of server-to-client payload that must accumulate on one connection before tcp.incoming.mode injects. Default 14, i.e. 14336 bytes. It is IGNORED in mode 'fake', which injects on every incoming data packet; only 'reset', 'fin' and 'desync' consult the threshold. 0 or a negative value does not mean 'fire immediately': at runtime it is replaced by 14 KB and forces tcp.incoming.max to 14 as well. Counting is per connection and restarts after every injection, so the mode fires repeatedly, once per threshold's worth of data. Footgun: incoming packets only reach b4 while the connection is still inside the queue.tcp_conn_bytes_limit window (default 19 packets - counted in the original direction by nftables, in the reply direction by iptables), so a threshold larger than the data that arrives inside that window never fires at all.
udp.conn_bytes_limit: Per-set count of PACKETS (not bytes) at the start of a UDP connection that should reach b4 - and it is DEAD: nothing in the packet path ever reads it. Default 8. Validate() clamps it down to queue.udp_conn_bytes_limit and the UI renders it as 'Connection Packets Limit' with that maximum, but the window that actually exists is built solely from queue.udp_conn_bytes_limit, as nftables 'ct original packets < N+1', as an iptables connbytes packets range 0:N, and as the TUN engine's own udpLimit. Changing this field therefore changes nothing about which packets b4 sees; raise queue.udp_conn_bytes_limit instead (it is floored at 8 and capped at 30).
udp.dport_filter: Comma-separated UDP destination ports and ranges, e.g. '443,5000-6000'; a colon is accepted and rewritten as a dash. Default '' - the set restricts nothing by port and contributes no ports. Validation rewrites the stored string and silently DROPS invalid entries, including any range whose start is not strictly below its end, so '443-443' vanishes. It does three jobs at once. Every enabled set's list, unioned with a hard-coded 443, becomes the kernel's UDP queue rule, so a UDP port other than 53 that no enabled set lists never reaches b4 at all. Port 53 is queued unconditionally and DNS is diverted before any set matching, so adding 53 here does nothing for DNS interception and only narrows this set's UDP matching to port 53. For a set that has IP or domain targets it NARROWS them: a packet to a port outside the list is not matched by IP, by learned IP or by SNI. And a set with no IP and no domain targets matches by port alone, which is the only way to build a port-only UDP set.
udp.fake_len: Payload size in BYTES of each decoy UDP packet in udp.mode 'fake'; the decoy copies the real packet's IP and UDP headers, uses faking.ttl, and carries this many payload bytes. Default 64; the UI offers 32-1500 in steps of 8 and nothing in validation clamps it. The payload named by udp.fake_payload_file is truncated or zero-padded to exactly this length, so the 1200- and 1357-byte presets are meaningless unless fake_len is raised to match. With '@quic_initial' the value goes straight into the generator, which returns nothing below 30 or above 16409 bytes and then the decoy is silently ZERO-FILLED instead of being a QUIC Initial; 1200 is the recommended size there. 0 produces header-only decoys. Cost is bandwidth multiplied by udp.fake_seq_length, on every matched packet.
udp.fake_payload_file: Body of each decoy UDP packet sent in udp.mode 'fake'. Default '' meaning no payload, so the decoy is udp.fake_len ZERO bytes. Three magic values are accepted besides a path: '@quic_initial' generates a fresh randomized QUIC Initial for every single decoy, with new random 8-byte connection IDs; '@preset:quic1' and '@preset:quic2' are captures compiled into the binary (1200 and 1357 bytes). Anything else is a FILE PATH RESOLVED AGAINST THE DIRECTORY HOLDING config.json, and it must stay inside that directory's captures/ subdirectory and end in .bin - so 'captures/quic_youtube_com.bin', never a bare filename and never an absolute path; a rejected or unreadable file logs an error and leaves the decoy zero-filled. Whatever is loaded is truncated or zero-padded to udp.fake_len, so a 1200-byte preset with the default fake_len of 64 puts only a 64-byte fragment of a QUIC header on the wire.
udp.fake_seq_length: How many decoy UDP packets are sent before the real one, on every matched packet, in udp.mode 'fake'. Despite the name it is a COUNT, not a sequence number or a length in bytes. Default 6; the UI offers 1-20. 0 sends no decoys but does NOT disable UDP processing: the original packet is still dropped and re-injected, and a QUIC Initial is still split into two IP fragments. A key omitted from config.json keeps the default 6, while an explicit 0 stays 0. Each decoy is followed by a udp.seg2delay sleep inside the injection goroutine, so count multiplied by delay is how long one injection slot is held; b4 allows 512 injections in flight and passes packets through unmodified once that is exhausted.
udp.faking_strategy: How the decoy UDP packets of udp.mode 'fake' are made unusable to the destination. Default 'none'. Only 'checksum' does anything: it inverts both bytes of each decoy's UDP checksum so the destination host discards them as corrupt after DPI on the path has already taken them into its per-flow state. 'ttl' is offered by the UI and the docs but is NEVER READ by the packet path - the decoy's TTL or hop limit always comes from faking.ttl (default 7) no matter what this is set to, so 'ttl' and 'none' behave identically. The value is not validated or normalised, so any other string also behaves as 'none'. Ignored unless udp.mode is 'fake'.
udp.filter_quic: Which QUIC counts as a match for this set: 'sni' (default) or 'all'. NormalizeQUICFilter rewrites EVERY other value to 'sni', including '', the legacy 'parse' and 'disabled', and the wrong-case 'ALL'. It never disables SNI parsing: b4 reads the SNI out of every long-header QUIC packet regardless of this setting, which is how a set learns domain-to-IP mappings. 'all' adds exactly one thing - a long-header QUIC packet sent to a destination this set ALREADY matches by IP target or by udp.dport_filter counts as a QUIC match even with no readable SNI. It does not widen the set to non-QUIC UDP or to unmatched destinations, and it changes nothing for udp.mode actions, which already fire on an IP or port match. Where it matters is block mode: a QUIC packet to an address the set only learned from an earlier ClientHello is blocked under 'all' and passed under 'sni'.
udp.filter_stun: Boolean, default true. When on, a matched packet whose payload is a STUN REQUEST (20-byte header, magic cookie 0x2112A442, request bits clear - responses and indications are deliberately not recognised) or a Discord voice packet (IP-discovery frame, or RTP version 2 with the Opus payload type) is accepted untouched and is never treated as handled. The check runs before udp.mode and before the routing block action, so it exempts voice media from drop, reject and block as well as from faking. Turning it off is what breaks Discord, Telegram and WhatsApp calls, which is exactly why it defaults on. Being a bool it is never restored by the defaults pass: an explicit false in the config stays false.
udp.mode: What b4 does with a UDP packet this set matched: 'off', 'fake', 'drop' or 'reject'. Default 'fake'. NormalizeUDPMode silently REWRITES any unrecognised value to that default, including '', 'none', 'disabled' and wrong case like 'Drop' - a typo therefore turns into active faking, never into pass-through. 'off' forwards the packet untouched but b4 still parses the QUIC ClientHello and records the SNI against the destination IP, so a set kept on 'off' keeps learning addresses. 'drop' discards it silently and the client falls back to TCP only after its own timeout; 'reject' discards it and sends ICMP port unreachable so the fallback is immediate. 'fake' drops the original and re-injects it from userspace, preceded by udp.fake_seq_length decoys and, when the payload is a long-header QUIC packet, split into two IP fragments. A set with routing.enabled true AND routing.mode 'block' is handled before this switch and ignores udp.mode entirely; routing.mode 'block' with routing.enabled left at its default false falls through and behaves normally.
udp.seg2delay: MILLISECONDS b4 sleeps after sending each decoy UDP packet, and between the two IP fragments of a split QUIC Initial. Default 0, which means no wait at all rather than some built-in gap. Together with udp.seg2delay_max it forms a min-max range resolved anew for each matched packet. The same pair is also reused, outside UDP faking, as the gap between the two fragments of a fragmented DNS query whenever dns.fragment_query is on, for both the UDP and the TCP DNS paths - so raising it for QUIC also slows DNS. Cost: the sleep happens in the injection goroutine and is paid once per decoy, so udp.fake_seq_length multiplies it; with 512 injections in flight allowed, long delays exhaust that budget and later packets go through unmodified.
udp.seg2delay_max: Upper bound in MILLISECONDS of the randomized UDP wait whose lower bound is udp.seg2delay. Default 0, and 0 means USE THE FIXED udp.seg2delay VALUE, not 'no maximum': the resolver returns min whenever max is less than or equal to min, so any max at or below min collapses to the fixed value and a max below min is ignored rather than swapped. Only max > min randomizes, uniformly over the inclusive range and re-rolled for every matched packet, which is what defeats DPI that fingerprints a constant inter-packet gap. Setting only this field while udp.seg2delay stays 0 gives a random 0-to-max wait. It bounds the fragmented-DNS gap as well, since that path shares the same two fields.
discovery.pipeline: Not a config setting: this is what b4's Discovery does, reachable over MCP as b4_find_bypass_strategy when 'Allow active probes' is on. It brute-forces bypass strategies against a real domain until one loads it. Order: a DNS poisoning probe, a baseline fetch with no bypass at all, cached presets that worked before, 18 Phase-1 presets, then per-family optimisation (the desync family alone is 120 presets), combinations, and finally confirmation, which re-fetches the winner several times in the shape it will be saved as. Each test pauses ~1.5s for the config to propagate and allows up to 5s for the fetch, so a run is minutes to tens of minutes, not seconds. Only one run exists at a time and the watchdog's self-healing shares the same runtime, so each blocks the other. Three outcomes must not be confused: baseline_works true means the domain loads WITHOUT b4 and no set should be created for it; transport_blocked means the address itself is unreachable, so no packet strategy can help and only a proxy or VPN route would; best_success false means nothing tried worked. Costs: it installs its own nftables steering rules and a second packet queue for the duration, defers watchdog healing, makes a firewall refresh wait up to five minutes, and emits heavy real traffic from the router. A finished run is written to discovery_history.json, which keeps one entry per domain (newest wins) together with the set the run built, so a winner can be applied later and after a restart, addressed by its suite id or just by the domain; the richer in-memory copy is dropped 30 seconds after the run ends, and applying from history carries the winning strategy but not the geo categories or addresses a live apply would have added.
